passages.happening:
The LORD asks Samuel how long he will go on mourning for Saul, since the LORD has rejected him as king. “Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have selected from his sons a king for Myself” (verse 1).

Samuel is afraid. “How can I go?” Samuel asked. “Saul will hear of it and kill me!” (verse 2). The LORD tells him to take a young cow and go to offer a sacrifice, to invite Jesse, and to anoint the one the LORD shows him (verses 2-3).

When Samuel comes to Bethlehem, the elders of the town come trembling to meet him: “Do you come in peace?” (verse 4). “In peace,” he replies. He has come to sacrifice. He tells them to make themselves ready and come, and he prepares Jesse and his sons himself (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 15 ended with Samuel mourning Saul and the LORD regretting that he had made him king. This chapter begins a new part of the story, the rise of David, which runs through the rest of 1 Samuel and into 2 Samuel, until David is king over all Israel.

Samuel's grief is real. God asks how long it will last, and then gives him a task.

Bethlehem was a small town in the hill country of Judah, about six miles south of the later Jerusalem. It was the town of Ruth and Boaz, and the book of Ruth traces David's family through them. David's reign is usually dated from about 1010 BC, so this anointing comes some years before, while Saul still reigns. How many years is not stated. David is still young enough to keep sheep.

Samuel's fear shows how badly things have broken down. Anointing another king while the king was alive was treason in any ancient kingdom. The elders tremble at the prophet's coming. They may simply have feared that a visit from such a man meant judgment, or they may have sensed the danger of being caught between Samuel and the king. The text does not say which.

The sacrifice is a real act of worship, and it gives a public reason for the family to gather. To consecrate the guests meant to have them get ready, by washing and avoiding what would make them unclean, before sharing a sacrificial meal.
passages.later:
The book of Ruth ends with this family's line: ‘they named him Obed. He became the father of Jesse, the father of David’ (Ruth 4:17).

Micah later promised a ruler for Israel from ‘Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah’ (Micah 5:2), and Matthew quotes that promise of Jesus' birth there: ‘for out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel’ (Matthew 2:6).
passages.asks: God asked Samuel how long he would mourn, and then gave him something to do. Ask whether there is a loss you need to grieve, and a task God may be giving you on the other side of it. And ask whether you are afraid, as Samuel was, of what obeying will cost.

passages.happening:
When they arrive, Samuel sees Eliab, Jesse's eldest, and thinks, “Surely here before the LORD is His anointed” (verse 6).

But the LORD stops him: “Do not consider his appearance or height, for I have rejected him; the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (verse 7).

Abinadab comes, and Shammah, and seven of Jesse's sons pass before Samuel. Each time Samuel says, ‘The LORD has not chosen any of these’ (verses 8-10). “Are these all the sons you have?” he asks. “There is still the youngest,” Jesse replied, “but he is tending the sheep” (verse 11). Samuel says they will not sit down to eat until he comes.

The boy is brought in. ‘He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance.’ The LORD says, “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one” (verse 12).

“So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the presence of his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. Then Samuel set out and went to Ramah” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The key word of the chapter is sight. Samuel saw Eliab. The LORD tells him not to look at appearance. Man looks on the outside, and the LORD sees the heart. In Hebrew the heart is the inner self, where thinking, choosing and loyalty happen.

The irony is sharp. Saul had been chosen as the tall, impressive man the people wanted. Now even Samuel judges by height, and God corrects him.

The sons pass by one at a time, slowly, and each time the answer is no. The repeating builds suspense before the youngest is sent for. His name is held back until the Spirit rushes upon him in verse 13, so his naming and his anointing come together.

In a world where the firstborn came first, choosing the youngest was a reversal on purpose. Genesis had already shown the pattern: Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph. Keeping sheep was ordinary work given to younger sons and servants. The feast waits for the boy nobody thought to call.

The Spirit rushes upon David with the same strong verb used of Samson and of Saul. But for David it is ‘from that day forward’, a lasting presence and not a burst of power for one battle.

Chronicles names seven sons of Jesse, with David the seventh, while this chapter seems to count eight. The difference has been explained in several ways, and the text does not settle it.
passages.later:
A psalm remembers the choice: “He chose David His servant and took him from the sheepfolds; from tending the ewes He brought him to be shepherd of His people Jacob, of Israel His inheritance” (Psalm 78:70-71).

Chronicles lists Jesse's sons in order, ending ‘Ozem sixth, and David seventh’ (1 Chronicles 2:15).
passages.asks: Samuel was sure the tall eldest son was the one. Ask when you have been certain about a person on the strength of how they looked, and what you learned later. And ask whom you have left out with the sheep, not thinking to call them in.

passages.t: A spirit of distress, and a boy with a harp
passages.happening:
“After the Spirit of the LORD had departed from Saul, a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him” (verse 14).

Saul's servants suggest a musician. Whenever the spirit troubles him, someone who plays the harp well can play, ‘and you will be well’ (verse 16). Saul tells them to find one (verse 17).

A servant has seen just the man: ‘a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp’, a brave warrior who speaks well and is handsome, ‘and the LORD is with him’ (verse 18). Saul sends for David, ‘who is with the sheep’, and Jesse sends him with a donkey loaded with bread, wine and a young goat (verses 19-20).

Saul likes David greatly, and David becomes his armor-bearer (verse 21). “And whenever the spirit from God came upon Saul, David would pick up his harp and play, and Saul would become well, and the spirit of distress would depart from him” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The chapter has two halves, and they mirror each other. In the first, the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon David. In the second, in the very next verse, the Spirit departs from Saul. The real handover of the kingship happens here, long before the public one.

In the Old Testament the Spirit often comes upon particular people to equip them for particular tasks. Saul's loss of the Spirit shows that, in this setting, the Spirit's power for an office could be taken away.

The word for distress literally means bad or harmful. It covers moral evil, and it also covers harm or misfortune, which is why translations vary between evil spirit and harmful spirit.

The harp was a small stringed instrument, more like a lyre than a modern harp. Music was widely thought to calm a troubled mind, and many ancient courts had musicians. The gifts Jesse sends were the usual courtesy when a son entered a greater man's service.

So God brings the chosen king into the rejected king's own house. The anointed boy from the sheep is now the one who soothes the man whose throne he will one day take.
passages.later: The Old Testament speaks of other spirits sent by God as judgment: ‘God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem’ (Judges 9:23), and in a prophet's vision a spirit goes out to deceive a king who would not listen (1 Kings 22:22).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that ‘a spirit of distress from the LORD’ tormented Saul? Does God send evil spirits?

The text says plainly that the spirit came from the LORD, and readers have understood it in several ways. Many see it as an evil spirit that God allowed or directed as judgment, as in other places where God uses hostile powers for his purposes, without being the author of evil himself. Others stress that the Hebrew word can mean harmful or troubling rather than morally evil, and understand it as an affliction of mind and spirit sent by God, while still treating it as judgment. Some readers hold both ideas. The Old Testament often traces all events, disasters included, back to God's rule without drawing the distinctions later theology would make.

What the text insists on is that Saul's torment follows the Spirit's departure, and that even here God gives relief through David's music.

The text does not name a condition, and it is wise not to diagnose one across three thousand years. No one should read this chapter and decide that another person's sorrow or illness is a spirit sent by God.

If sadness has settled on you and will not lift, these verses do not shame you. When grief or sadness lasts and starts taking sleep, appetite or work, seeing a doctor is wise, and it is not a failure of faith. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone now: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: David's music brought Saul relief, even though Saul would later turn on him. Ask whose burden you could ease with a gift you already have. And ask whether you are willing to serve someone whose place you might one day be given.
